paras.en: Trevor, who plays Dibz, is such an amazing and brave actor. But it was definitely always safety first. In no way was I willing to traumatize any crew or cast members by making this film, and in no way were we trying to put anybody’s lives in physical danger. We said if anything sketchy happens, we’d regroup at a meeting point. So we had precautions in place. There were a couple of people, as we were shooting throughout the day, who were like, “Why do you have such a large camera? What are you guys doing?” And we just said, “Oh, we’re an independent outlet,” and they loved the idea that we weren’t the corporate media.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In Pop Pop, we see some modern-looking scenes in the cyber sphere but also an older-looking computer with its loud typing sounds and retro-feeling pop-up windows and the like. Can you explain how important it was for you that the technology side of the story of the film was reflected by the visual experience?

I always love to ask what the organizing principle of a story is. I thought of this computer screen almost as a character to start priming the audience for the rules of that kind of existence. The idea was to put this device into this story that’s a deeply digital one.

And the digital space is a mix of stuff that we made up and actual memes. There are memes that would have been popular in 2016. There’s a Drake dancing, there’s Obama, they’re flying over what’s called the political compass, which is a meme that lets you self-locate where you are politically, and then there are some more obscure gems. My biggest dream for this movie is, and I’ll know I have made it then, that somebody writes a listicle called “25 Memes That You Can See in Pop Pop.”
Since you just mentioned the title again, how did you choose that?

To me, it was about the feeling of everything breaking apart. My generation in the States grew up with this idea that institutions were healthy and that there were certain social contracts that would never be broken. But we have seen in the past 12-plus years that there’s been a giant pickaxe that has been taken to that version of reality. So, the title is in reference to that breaking down and that combustible tinderbox energy of everything just sort of blowing up.

But it is also that this is pop filmmaking, which is about swallowing everything and metabolizing it so it becomes this different thing. Here’s all this imagery – let’s put it through the wringer and talk about it, interrogate it, and see where we land. So it’s a little bit of an accidental double entendre.
You say double entendre, so I need to ask you about that great double act that your two leads are. And Lena and the others give it all a real ensemble vibe.

These brilliant young actors are giving incredible performances. I cannot wait for people to see them. They are amazing. I really hope that we can introduce people to them. I am so excited for people to see them for the first time.
I assume you didn’t have a huge budget and didn’t win the lottery?

No, I worked to pay the bills and keep the lights on, producing big events for brands [and things like that as a day job]. I just kept Tetris-ing every single job I possibly could into my schedule without going absolutely insane. I was doing crazy shit, including following a giant Bath & Body Works candle around the Eastern Seaboard or going to the Grove in L.A. telling people to use circular Legos, not the square ones. I also got really lucky in that my collaborators were really down and kept coming back to this project time and time again.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I think this was true indie filmmaking. The hope and dream is that, as we watch in our industry all of these conglomerates sell to each other and combine forces, what happens is a healthier indie undercurrent, so that films like this and filmmakers who have ideas that are a little bit more out there can get their films made with less strife than five years of Tetris-ing so many jobs together.
In the “thank you” section of the credits, I saw the name Zazie Beetz. Is that THE Zazie Beetz?
Yes, she and her now-husband David [Rysdahl] did some very early development on this film.
After I watched Pop Pop, I felt motivated to try harder again to keep in dialogue with people who may not always share my political or other ideas or hopes. What’s your hope for audiences of Pop Pop?

I hope it causes massive fights and wrecks entire families. No, I’m kidding! (laughs) I really set out to make a movie about people who are right when they’re wrong and wrong when they’re right and what it means to be morally three-dimensional in a world that provides us with not many great options for being a good person.

So, yes, I wanted to ask how we deal with other people who we potentially don’t agree with, but we still have to be in community with. It’s really about thinking seriously about community building and coalition building. I think one of the things that this country has to do is to figure out how we can build coalitions, and part of that is joining hands with people that we don’t necessarily always agree with and figuring out what is still left in the concentric circles between us.

It’s my hope that folks can utilize the film as a jumping-off point to talk about their own struggles. A lot of us are about to go home for Thanksgiving and have anxiety-inducing political conversations around the family table. Perhaps, once you see this movie, instead of pointing to your uncle with whom you disagree, or fighting with your mother, you can look at these characters and use them as ciphers to have discussions instead of pointing fingers.
I’m hungry for other filmmakers to go out there and make films that really are responding to and rising to meet the moment, and I want to meet them.

articles.title: Stock futures edge lower after markets slide amid Nvidia woes: Live updates

paras.en: U.S. equity futures edged lower early Friday after major indexes declined and Nvidia shares fell, following the exit of its founder and CEO Jensen Huang amid an ongoing scandal.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were marginally down, while S&P 500 futures were down 0.12%. Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.38%.

The action comes after the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 dropped about 0.4% each in regular trading. The Dow slid almost 190 points, or 0.4%. Nvidia's 4.3% decline dragged down the three major averages, even as the chip stock ended the session off its lows.

Asia-Pacific markets were mostly lower, with South Korea's Kospi down 0.85% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index down 1.4%. Mainland China's CSI 300 declined 0.66%. Japan's Nikkei 225 bucked the trend to rise 0.53%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.62%.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from his post at the chip company following reported extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.

Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress, who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.

A jump in oil prices also kept stocks under pressure Thursday, with Brent crude rising more than 3% on the day to settle at $95.82 a barrel. Oil climbed after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post, "We don't need a deal with Iran." The comment raised concerns that the U.S.-Iran war could drag on further.

Another market catalyst awaits on Friday in the form of October's producer price index reading, a measure of wholesale inflation. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline PPI rising 0.4% on the month and 6.6% from 12 months earlier.

Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up 3.2%, while the S&P 500 is on pace for a 2.9% advance. The Dow is poised for a nearly 2% jump. All three indexes are heading for their best weekly performances since early August.

articles.title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services

paras.en: Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday that impacted users around the world.

The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. External services that connect with Outlook features such as Calendar also experienced issues.

Email and other tools were unavailable for Microsoft users through much of the Asian business day and into the early European hours. In an update just before 6:20 a.m. in London (1:20 a.m. ET), Microsoft said "Users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services," including Outlook on either web or desktop, and did not give a timeline for restoring service.

"As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident. We will continue to treat this incident with urgency and priority until full resolution," Microsoft said, adding that it would provide a full report with further details once the problem was mitigated.
It also said that as part of efforts to recover its frontend service, it was "evaluating traffic controls that can be applied to increase capacity and stability."
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m. Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."
Microsoft initially said infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions" was responsible for the connectivity problems.

The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure" and that some servers were failing automated health checks.
"We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service," Microsoft wrote.

articles.title: Why Singapore keeps turning up in the fight over Nvidia chips and China

paras.en: Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.

The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country.

A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday.

Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.
The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development.

Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.
Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up.

Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year.
Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering.

Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added.
"Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said.
Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators.
Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation.
Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement.

The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said.
Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025.

In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.

The country does not enforce "unilateral export controls" imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday's statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities.

Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.

Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company.

Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis.
Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

articles.title: Was Isaac Newton’s contribution to calculus stolen?

paras.en: Humanity has pondered infinities since time immemorial. It has even tried to define them: What happens, for example, if you continually increase a number by one? Is it possible to eventually reach a value that exceeds all natural numbers? For that matter, what happens if you make the absolute value of a number ever smaller?

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The oldest known records of such considerations come from Archimedes, who lived in the third century B.C.E. But infinities and their opposites, infinitely tiny values called infinitesimals, became truly significant in the 17th century, spurring one of the most intense scientific debates the world had ever seen.

In the 1660s and 1670s, both Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz laid the foundations for what we now call calculus. This branch of mathematics deals with measuring geometric figures and investigating variable quantities, among other things.

At that time, Newton was conducting research at Trinity College Cambridge. Then, in 1665, the bubonic plague swept across Europe, forcing the university to close its doors. Newton dedicated himself even more intensely to his research during this period, making impressive strides in optics and kinematics and even developing a theory of gravitation.
The young physicist was particularly fascinated by variable systems. To describe these, however, he needed a new kind of mathematics—which Newton, then in his 20s, invented for this purpose.

Imagine you drop a ball to the ground. Its velocity will increase over time as the Earth’s gravitational pull accelerates it. The distance, s, traveled by the ball can be described by the equation of motion s = 1/2 gt², where grepresents the acceleration due to gravity, which is 9.81 meters per second squared near Earth’s surface. To keep the formulas as concise as possible, we will omit units and approximate g as 10. This gives us an approximate result of s ≈ 5t² in meters for the distance traveled.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But what if we want to know the ball’s speed after it has traveled for one second? We know that the average velocity, v, of an object over a distance traveled is given by the time it takes to travel that distance: v = s/t . But what if the velocity changes continuously and we are interested in v(t) at a specific time, t?

Newton realized that the result for the instantaneous velocity becomes more accurate when the time interval from which the value is calculated is smaller. To this end, he eventually introduced an “infinitesimal” quantity (dt, in modern notation), which corresponds to a tiny time interval—smaller than any ordinary number.

The velocity at time t = 1 could therefore be calculated by dividing the distance traveled between t = 1 and t = 1 + dt, written as s(1 + dt) – s(1), by the time interval dt. Substituting the values for t into the distance formula, we obtain: s(1 + dt) = 5(1 + dt)2 = 5 + 10dt + 5(dt)2 and s(t = 1) = 5.
Thus, for the velocity, v, at time t = 1, it follows that: v(t = 1) = (s(1+dt)−s(1)) / dt = (10dt + 5(dt)2) / dt = 10 + 5dt.
What does this result, which still depends on dt, mean? According to Newton, it’s 10 meters per second: he simply omitted the dt term.

About a decade later, philosopher Leibniz considered similar ideas—albeit for entirely different reasons. He was looking for a way to calculate the area under a curve. To do this, he divided the area into increasingly smaller intervals to approximate it by summing the areas of numerous rectangular shapes. The narrower the intervals, the more accurate the calculation becomes. And so Leibniz, too, introduced an infinitesimal: dx.

More detailed investigations of such infinitesimal calculations were then sidelined by a dispute between Leibniz and Newton. Although Leibniz had published his theory before his English colleague, a supporter of Newton—and later Newton himself—claimed that Leibniz had seen his unpublished work on infinitesimal calculus beforehand and had stolen his ideas.

The British Royal Society subsequently launched an investigation that said it had confirmed Newton’s accusations. But Newton himself was president of the society and hand-picked the investigating committee. (Newton, for all his intelligence, is also remembered for ruthlessness; he attacked other brilliant contemporaries, including scientist Robert Hooke.)
Leibniz’s reputation was ruined. He died in 1716, and his grave was unmarked. Only about 75 years later did people add the inscription “OSSA LEIBNITII” (meaning “the bones of Leibniz”).

Today historians of science agree that there were significant differences between Leibniz’s and Newton’s work on calculus, concluding that both scientists had probably arrived at their findings independently of each other.
Next time, I’ll dig into the controversy within the mathematical community surrounding the concept of infinitesimals.

articles.title: This asteroid was born at the dawn of the solar system

paras.en: Most carbon-rich meteorites are studded with the remnants of molten droplets from the birth of the solar system. These ubiquitous millimeter-size beads of rock, called chondrules, come from the disk of material that surrounded the newborn sun 4.6 billion years ago. Yet the asteroid Ryugu, or at least the parts sampled by Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft, contains almost none of them. Research published recently in Science suggests Ryugu may be so incredibly old that it formed before the chondrules did, making it part of the very first generation of planetesimals—small bodies that act as planetary precursors—to form in the solar system.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To determine Ryugu’s age, researchers probed the samples for a mineral called dolomite, which can carry radioactive manganese that slowly turns into chromium; the proportions of related elements let researchers calculate when in the early solar system the dolomite formed. They also measured the balance of heavy and light oxygen atoms in minerals that had crystallized in the samples. Cool water loads a growing crystal with more of the heavy form, and that preference fades as the water warms, so the contrast between neighboring minerals reveals how hot the water was. Based on these two metrics, the team found one Ryugu grain containing dolomite that formed at about 92 degrees Celsius some 4.565 billion years ago.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The heat required to form the dolomite came from within the asteroid’s parent body and would have taken at least a million years to build, says study co-author Ann Nguyen, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Accounting for that necessary heating process, the researchers’ simulations suggest the asteroid came together less than two million years after the solar system’s first solids—before most chondrules.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The finding fits theories that planets and other bodies in the solar system were built in waves as a mixture of fine dust, ice, organic matter and specks of stardust circling the newborn sun clumped together into ever larger objects. The first generation of planetesimals appeared within about a million years of the first solid grains, and later ones came a few million years afterward, when chondrules were ubiquitous. If the study’s results are correct, Ryugu could be a leftover of that first wave. Planet building, it seems, began almost as soon as the solar system did, and some asteroids still preserve its raw ingredients.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “This study is really interesting and has a high impact for the field,” says Myriam Telus, a planetary scientist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, who was not involved in the work. She notes, though, that other dating methods have put the first chondrules earlier in the solar system’s history and that the manganese-chromium dating system the researchers used still needs to be refined. Regardless, it’s clear Ryugu formed very early in the system’s history, the scientists agree.

Next Nguyen and her colleagues will apply their methods to asteroid Bennu, sampled by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission, and Nguyen hopes to report the results soon. Comparing Bennu with Ryugu “will help us constrain whether they could have come from the same parent asteroid,” Nguyen adds—and whether the two could be siblings from the dawn of the solar system.

articles.title: Why did a Brooklyn building collapse so suddenly? Experts weigh in

paras.en: The devastating collapse of a Brooklyn building on Wednesday that has left at least eight people dead and more than a dozen injured may have been primarily caused by a failure to properly shore up soil at a neighboring construction site, according to multiple experts.

The incident, which occurred at around 4 P.M. EST in the Flatbush neighborhood, saw the building give way into the construction site. City officials on Thursday said rescue operations are ongoing and urged the public to stay away from the area.

A New York City Department of Buildings spokesperson said the department would conduct an investigation into the exact cause of the collapse, including “comprehensive reviews of the records and site conditions” at the fallen building and neighboring site. The developers responsible for the construction site have active permits for excavation and foundation work, the spokesperson said.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

It is possible that work may have disturbed the soil around the foundation of the destroyed apartment building. While pictures indicate that a shoring system had been used to hold that soil in place, that shoring may have failed, says Michael Chajes, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Delaware.

“If there’s work going on and there’s extreme vibration, I suspect it was undermining the existing structure, causing a redistribution of forces, and causing a collapse is probably the most likely thing,” Chajes says.

Shoring or bracing are a commonplace safety strategies during construction work. They can consist of steel piles driven into the perimeter of the construction site, with some form of board between them, forming a temporary wall that keeps soil from caving in, Chajes explains.

“The tricky thing is when you’re right up against a neighboring building like this is there’s extra soil that’s adjacent to it that you’re trying to keep from caving into your construction site,” says Gregory Deierlein, a civil and environmental engineer at Stanford University. “That’s under high pressure from the building next door, so the wall needs to be stiff enough that it doesn’t allow the soil to deform or yield a little bit.”

The design of the bracing needs to take into account the kind of soil in the area, as well as the weight of the neighboring building and that building’s foundation. Failure to do so accurately can cause weaknesses that mean even minor factors, such as an increase in rainfall in the area, can cause the soil to soften and shift, placing increased pressure on one side of a structure and causing it to give way.
Shoring can also be disturbed by vibrations from heavy machinery that’s typical in construction sites, says Mehrdad Sasani, a civil engineering professor at Northeastern University.

“At the same time, the building was an old building, and the integrity of that building could have also played a secondary role in this process,” he adds. “It’s likely the structure was not well integrated and sensitive to any amount of movement caused by lack of proper shoring, and that led to collapse.”

The DOB did not offer a timeline for its investigation; Sasani says the department will likely conclude it was a combination of factors that led to the deadly collapse. The construction site’s developer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"There are codes and regulations—and codes and regulations, if properly followed, often we don’t see collapses,” he says. “Collapses occur because of not following the standards here and there and often is a combination of several factors.”

articles.title: This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor
articles.author: Allie Skalnik

paras.en: Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

articles.title: This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize
articles.author: Carolyn Gramling

paras.en: The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

articles.title: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice
articles.author: Katherine Kornei

paras.en: Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

articles.title: The Number of Teeth in Your Mouth Could Be a Major Warning Sign of Dementia
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: We still don't fully understand the causes of dementia, but scientists are making progress.

Most encouragingly, research suggests that almost half of dementia cases could be reduced, at least temporarily, thanks to modifiable risk factors that can help to prevent or postpone the disease from occurring.
But a new study reveals we might have been overlooking a serious risk factor for cognitive decline, and it's been hiding right under our nose.
According to a study in the Journal of the American Medical Directors Association, poor oral health could be a much greater contributor to dementia than we ever realized.

While a number of studies have linked oral health to dementia, it wasn't included as one of 14 modifiable risk factors in the influential Lancet Commission findings updated in 2024, which in turn helped to inform new WHO guidelines released this year on dementia risk reduction.
That might bear some rethinking, based on new evidence uncovered by scientists in Japan.

In the study, researchers analyzed data from 47,293 adults aged 65 or older who took part in the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study (JAGES), following the participants for approximately nine years, from 2013 to 2022.

During that follow-up period, 8,247 (17.4 percent) of the participants developed dementia, and the researchers wanted to investigate the extent to which poor oral health – measured by teeth count – was linked to dementia,
compared to the established risk factors listed by the Lancet Commission (excluding two that couldn't be assessed using JAGES data: high LDL cholesterol and air pollution).

"We used the number of remaining teeth as an indicator of poor oral health, as tooth loss generally reflects the end point of a lifelong oral disease history, such as advanced dental caries and severe periodontal disease," the research team, including first author and medical student Maho Iwata from Tohoku University, explains in their paper.

In their analysis, the researchers found that having fewer teeth was linked to a significantly higher incidence of dementia, increasing from an incidence rate of 1.63 (per 100 person-years) for people with 20 or more teeth, to 2.31 (for 10–19 teeth), 2.97 (for 1–9 teeth), and 4.34 (for people with no remaining teeth).

After adjusting for sex, age, and equivalent income, dementia risk was found to increase with fewer teeth, being 14 percent higher for people with 10–19 teeth, 12 percent higher for 1–9 teeth, and 27 percent higher for no teeth, compared to individuals with 20 or more teeth.
But the most striking finding came when the researchers compared poor oral health to the modifiable risk factors recognized by the Lancet Commission.

Using a statistical method called population attributable fractions (PAFs) to estimate how much risk factors might contribute to disease across a population if they played a causal role, the researchers calculated a PAF of 7.2 percent for tooth loss – meaning it could account for 7.2 percent of the cases of dementia in the study.

What's surprising is that, over the total population, that 7.2 percent estimate was the third largest PAF overall, following only depressive symptoms (which hypothetically accounted for 10.5 percent of dementia cases) and social isolation (9.4 percent).

Even more remarkably, when the results were filtered by men only, tooth loss had the single largest PAF out of every risk factor in the study (at 12 percent), whereas for women, it was the fourth largest (6.1 percent).

That's quite a finding, and the researchers say it suggests that tooth loss may account for a greater share of dementia cases than known risk factors such as physical inactivity, smoking, and low education.

"To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify and compare the PAFs of poor oral health and a large number of other risk factors for dementia within the same population framework," the team writes.

"In particular, in men, the PAF for tooth loss in our study was substantial and comparable to the top-ranked modifiable risk factors, such as depressive symptoms and social isolation, reported by the Lancet Commission, indicating its relatively large contribution to dementia onset."
The researchers acknowledge a number of limitations with the study, including that the JAGES data relies on self-reported information from participants, which may be prone to bias or errors.

It's also worth noting that PAFs are speculative, and even though the method estimates how risk factors might contribute to disease, the study doesn't actually demonstrate that tooth loss causes dementia, or that preventing tooth loss would necessarily prevent dementia cases.

That said, the team says there are several pathways that could support the link. Having fewer teeth could impact the ability to chew and eat food, which could lead to poor nutrition, which is linked to cognitive decline.

Losing your teeth is also linked to social isolation, which is another risk factor for dementia. And tooth loss is also related to oral inflammation, which may lead to systemic inflammation, which can drive cognitive decline.

While more research is needed, the study authors say their findings show that oral health has major public health implications, urging that it should be integrated into dementia prevention strategies.

"This study demonstrates that tooth loss makes a substantial contribution to dementia incidence, comparable to major established modifiable risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission," the researchers conclude.
"Together with the growing body of evidence, these findings argue for re-evaluating oral health as a key dementia risk factor and for its inclusion in future updates of the Lancet Commission report."
The findings are reported in the Journal of the American Medical Directors Association.

articles.title: Physicists Say They've Sidestepped a Nearly 100-Year-Old Quantum Limit Using Hindsight
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle, introduced by German physicist Werner Heisenberg in 1927, puts forward the concept of a certain fuzziness in physics. It says that if one characteristic of a quantum particle can be predicted with precision, a paired characteristic becomes less certain.

Position and momentum are the most often-mentioned of these pairs, known as non-commuting variables. Being able to ascertain where a quantum particle is makes it harder to judge its movement, and vice versa.

That fuzziness makes it more difficult to take accurate measurements of weaker signals in physics – in everything from the LIGO gravitational wave detector to the atomic clocks that underpin systems like GPS.
Now researchers led by a team from Shanxi University in China think they've found a fundamental workaround, and it involves looking backward into the past, as well as ahead into the future.

"We experimentally demonstrate simultaneous estimation of non-commuting variables beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty bound and verify the results using weak measurement," write the researchers in a preprint version of their paper, which has yet to be peer-reviewed.

Rather than making a prediction of the future to take a measurement, the researchers wanted to test an alternative approach: taking a measurement using data from both before and after the point to be measured.

The hypothesis was that the two-way perspective should remove some of the fuzziness in observations. It was put to the test using 52 billion rubidium atoms collected in a small glass chamber, with a laser used to line up their spins (magnetic properties).
As the spin alignment caused the atoms to behave as one quantum system, the momentum and position of which could then be measured by a second laser.

Using readings from both before and after improved the accuracy of the system's predictions, by a modest amount – they were around 20 percent more precise than the Heisenberg uncertainty limit allows.

"The central ingredient of this approach is the consistent incorporation of both past and future measurement information to refine the inference of the system state at a given time," write the researchers.
Measurements were taken continuously for 84 minutes, and the setup enabled the researchers to measure both position and momentum simultaneously. The usual trade-off between the two was eased.

Of course, waiting until after something has happened to measure it means you're limited in terms of real-time monitoring, but the strengths of the new technique and the greater accuracy may outweigh whatever disadvantages there are.
"This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies," write the researchers.

In a lot of quantum systems – including the atomic clocks mentioned earlier – retrospective readings are the norm anyway, so scientists wouldn't necessarily slow down the analysis using the new approach.

It means we could be looking at more accurate quantum sensors coming online in the future, and may be getting greater insight into future quantum research findings, now that we know how the before-and-after status of a system can work in tandem.

The researchers are still keen to improve the experimental setup further, with more precise instrumentation and more accurate readings. Adding in the concept of quantum entanglement could be one way forward.

Importantly, Heisenberg's limit on the uncertainty of a quantum system still applies (which is good news – it underpins a lot of fundamental physics theory). What this study shows is that the principle can be circumvented to some extent, by working out probabilities in a different way.

"Over the past century, this seminal theoretical framework has not only served as a critical component in the interpretation of quantum mechanics but has also revolutionized our conceptual understanding of measurement limitations at the quantum scale," write the researchers.
The research is not yet peer-reviewed, but a preprint is available online at arXiv.

articles.title: Hundreds of Stone Age Rock Carvings Found Hidden in Plain Sight in a Spanish Cave
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: A trove of Paleolithic cave art has been hiding in plain sight.
People have been walking through the Cova de la Font Major, a cave system in Catalonia, northeastern Spain, very regularly in the past century.

Ever since the entrance to the cave was cleared in 1957, countless cave enthusiasts, treasure hunters looking for bronze artifacts, and more recently, tourists, have trod through its limestone caverns.

But it wasn't until 2019 that Josep Maria Vergès, a researcher at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, encountered a series of parallel lines that hinted at just how long humans have been making their subterranean marks in the cave.
Catalonia has mostly been a dead zone for rock art, next to a region that is otherwise world-renowned for its rich collections of Paleolithic relics.
The discovery at Cova de la Font Major changes that.
Vergès and his colleague, archaeologist Míriam Salas-Altès, have since documented 280 different Paleolithic motifs etched into the walls of a chamber called the Gatoneres de Cal Palletes.
Cova de la Font Major, it turns out, contains the third-largest known assemblage of ice age cave art in Mediterranean Iberia.

"For more than six decades, thousands of visitors passed directly in front of the engraved surfaces, and in some cases inscribed names and dates over them, without the Paleolithic origin of the figures being recognized," Vergès says.

"Along the Iberian Mediterranean facade, from the Pyrenees to Gibraltar, around 75 percent of known assemblages contain no more than five zoomorphic figures, and over 90 percent contain no more than 20," adds Salas-Altès.
"The sheer quantity of art discovered at the Cova de la Font Major is therefore particularly exceptional."
Among the 55 animal figures are horses, deer, goats, cattle, an auroch, and even a bear, though several others could not be identified.

But some of the graphics are more abstract: the fence-like rows of upright parallel lines, for instance, and an intriguing composition of intricate looped shapes that almost look like a kind of writing, though the researchers say it's not yet clear how old these loops are.
"Contrary to what was previously thought, northeastern Iberia holds first-rate Paleolithic rock art sites," Salas-Altès says.

"The Mediterranean art of western Europe is now enriched by a new body of rock art, which allows us to characterize in greater depth a Mediterranean graphic tradition with an identity of its own, distinct from that of the Franco-Cantabrian region."

The researchers believe the rock art could predate the Magdalenian culture, but that's still a best guess on its age. They're planning to undertake uranium dating using calcite deposited on one of the animal depictions.
Even before the cave was rediscovered in 1853, there's evidence humans have been in and out of the Cova de la Font Major through various periods in history.
Charcoal and a flint-backed bladelet indicate human presence in the Upper Paleolithic.
A human femur, dated to the late Neolithic, suggests one section was used for burial.

And then there was the hoard of Bronze Age artifacts sealed safely within, from the moment when a collapse closed the cave's entrance, probably during the Roman period, until the 20th-century treasure hunters arrived.
Since 1993, the cave has been maintained as a kind of subterranean museum, restricting access to the Gatoneres.
But from 1957 onwards, modern humans had already done a fair bit of damage to the cave art.
The Gatoneres suffered significant damage in those few decades, in the form of erosion that comes from bodies brushing against the walls, and graffiti.
Vergès and Salas-Altès suspect there were once many more Paleolithic etchings that have been lost as a result.
Parts of the Cova de la Font Major remain open to the public, but the section containing the carvings is closed to protect the art from further damage.
The research has been published in Antiquity.

articles.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

paras.en: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

- A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.
Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.
Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.
Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.
These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.
Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Miika M. Wynne-Ellis, Heli E. K. Virtanen, Elizabeth Bertone-Johnson, Sari Hantunen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, Jukka T. Salonen, Jyrki K. Virtanen. Associations of dietary proteins with serum total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations in middle-aged men. International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, 2026; 77 (6): 576 DOI: 10.1080/09637486.2026.2731397

articles.title: A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

paras.en: A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

- Researchers at Brown University have overcome a major obstacle to creating ultra-low-power computer chips that could help slash the energy demands of AI. Their breakthrough eliminates a long-standing "dead layer" problem that causes promising materials to stop working when made extremely thin. Remarkably, the new technique not only preserves the materials' electrical and magnetic properties at nearly atomic thicknesses but also gives them enhanced magnetic capabilities

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."
The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.
Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.
How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer
To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.
That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.
Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.
But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.
This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

paras.en: In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.
The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.
A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing
As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."
